findings.paper_title: SM 2627 Q1 TM Update App A 21-07-26
findings.headline: The council is deliberately using internal borrowing from cash reserves to avoid expensive medium- to long-term external debt while rates remain high.
findings.detail: Rather than locking into long-term PWLB loans at current elevated rates (5.00% for 5-year, 5.50% for 10-year), the council is funding capital spending from spare cash balances and only taking short-term external borrowing. This strategy depends on rates falling to avoid eventually taking out expensive long-term debt.
findings.matters: Internal borrowing depletes the council's liquid reserves and creates refinancing risk if rates do not fall, potentially forcing expensive external borrowing later.
findings.figures: 5yr PWLB rate: 5.00%. 10yr PWLB rate: 5.50%. Short-term loan rate: 4.25% (6 months).
findings.quote: PWLB and intra-local authority external borrowing interest rates are also expected to be higher than at budget setting, which continues to restrict the opportunity to take medium to long term external debt. The practice continues to avoid medium to long term borrowing commitments by utilising spare cash balances as internal funding, or short-term borrowing with a view to reviewing borrowing requirements should the rates begin to decrease.

findings.paper_title: SM 2627 Q1 TM Update App A 21-07-26
findings.headline: Investment income is projected to fall £100k short of budget as higher rates are offset by lower cash balances from internal borrowing.
findings.detail: The council budgeted to receive £626,130 in investment income in 2026/27, assuming interest rates would fall. Whilst rates have remained higher, the investment portfolio has shrunk due to internal borrowing and cash flow fluctuations, resulting in a net shortfall of £100k.
findings.matters: Lower-than-expected investment returns reduce the council's capacity to self-fund services and increase dependency on borrowing or reserves.
findings.figures: Budgeted investment income: £626,130. Forecast shortfall: £100,000. Average portfolio balance: £13.8m. Quarter-end portfolio: £14.8m.
findings.quote: The Council has budgeted to receive £626,130 in investment income in 2026/27 based on the expectation of reducing interest rates over the year. Whilst interest rates have remained higher so far in the year, the size of investment portfolio is impact by continued internal borrowing and other cash flow fluctuations. A shortfall of £100,000 is forecast against this budget but is subject to change based on these factors throughout the year.

findings.paper_title: SM 2627 Q1 TM Update App A 21-07-26
findings.headline: External borrowing has increased from £12.1m to forecast £17m to fund the capital programme.
findings.detail: The council took a new £5m loan in April 2026 at 4.25% for 6 months and is forecasting year-end borrowing of £17m. This 40% increase funds the capital programme net financing need of £11.3m. All borrowing remains within the operational boundary (£33.5m) and authorised limit (£35.5m).
findings.matters: A significant single-year increase in external debt changes the council's leverage and debt service costs, material to any lending decision.
findings.figures: Opening borrowing: £12.1m. New loan: £5m at 4.25% (6 months). Forecast year-end: £17m. Operational boundary: £33.501m. Authorised limit: £35.501m.
findings.quote: The Council's external borrowing outstanding at 31 March 2026 was £12.1million. A new loan of £5million was taken in April at 4.25% for 6 months. Borrowing at the end of the year is forecast to be £17million but remains under review to support the general fund underlying borrowing need.

findings.paper_title: SM 2627 Q1 TM Update App A 21-07-26
findings.headline: Interest rates have not fallen as budget assumed, affecting both borrowing costs and investment returns.
findings.detail: The budget was set expecting the Bank of England base rate to fall to 3.50% by end of Q1 and 3.25% by end of Q3. The latest forecast shows no decrease — rates remain at 3.75% for the whole financial year. PWLB rates are also higher than anticipated, restricting external borrowing opportunities.
findings.matters: A sustained higher interest rate environment increases the council's debt servicing costs and reduces investment returns, directly squeezing the general fund budget.
findings.figures: Base rate: 3.75% (no change expected). Budgeted rate decreases: to 3.50% (Q1), then 3.25% (Q3). 5yr PWLB: 5.00%. 10yr PWLB: 5.50%.
findings.quote: The latest forecast does not expect any further decrease in this financial year. The budget was set with the assumption that there would be two decreases during the year, to 3.50% by the end of quarter 1 and 3.25% by the end of quarter 3.

findings.paper_title: Internal Audit Annual Report
findings.headline: Four service areas received limited assurance ratings for internal controls
findings.detail: Internal Audit assessed control effectiveness across 32 audited service areas. Four service areas received 'limited assurance' ratings, meaning weaknesses in control systems or non-compliance with controls put achievement of system objectives at risk. Two areas achieved substantial assurance and 26 achieved satisfactory assurance; zero areas received unsatisfactory ratings.
findings.matters: Control weaknesses identified across multiple service areas suggest potential gaps in risk management and financial oversight that could affect council operations and creditworthiness
findings.figures: 4 service areas limited assurance, 26 satisfactory assurance, 2 substantial assurance, 0 unsatisfactory assurance
findings.quote: 4 service areas had controls within the system to provide limited assurance that risks material to the achievement of the systems objectives are adequately managed

findings.paper_title: Risk Management Update
findings.headline: Staff Resources and Employee Wellbeing identified as high-rated strategic risks
findings.detail: Both staff resources and employee wellbeing appear on the strategic risk matrix as high-impact, medium-high likelihood risks. These are listed without further explanation in this summary document.
findings.matters: Staff capacity and retention risks can impact service delivery, speed of response to audit issues, and ability to execute savings plans or capital projects
findings.figures: 2 of 10 high-rated strategic risks; both high impact / medium-high likelihood
findings.quote: - Staff Resources  - Employee wellbeing

findings.paper_title: Risk Management Update
findings.headline: Renters Rights Act creating high-impact, high-likelihood strategic risk
findings.detail: New legislation on renter protections is mapped on the strategic risk matrix as high impact and high likelihood. The paper does not detail the specific financial or operational exposure to the council.
findings.matters: New regulatory requirement with high-impact exposure suggests either new statutory duties or new costs the council must absorb, affecting financial sustainability
findings.figures: Renters Right Act rated high impact / high likelihood on strategic risk matrix
findings.quote: - Renters Right Act

findings.paper_title: Risk Management Update
findings.headline: Council-controlled company AES carrying 9 high-rated risks
findings.detail: AES (a wholly-owned and controlled company) has 9 high-rated and 5 medium-rated risks. The paper states these are now being included in council risk reporting for greater visibility of overall risk exposure.
findings.matters: Material exposure through council-controlled entities affects consolidated financial risk and debt covenants; 9 high-rated risks suggests significant active issues requiring management
findings.figures: AES: 9 high, 5 medium rated risks
findings.quote: AES: 9 high, 5 medium rated risks

findings.paper_title: Risk Management Update
findings.headline: Medium Term Financial Plan identified as high-rated strategic risk
findings.detail: The MTFP appears on the Council's strategic risk matrix as a high-impact, medium-high likelihood risk. Without the appendix detail, the specific nature of the financial planning risk is not stated in this summary.
findings.matters: MTFP is the council's primary tool for managing multi-year finances and debt sustainability; flagging it as high-rated suggests financial planning capability or assumptions at risk
findings.figures: 10 high-rated strategic risks of 21 identified; MTFP mapped as high impact / medium-high likelihood
findings.quote: The ten high rated risks are mapped on Matrix 1 below... - MTFP

findings.paper_title: Risk Management Update
findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation decision imminent with 6 high-rated risks to financial planning and service continuity
findings.detail: The LGR proposal was submitted in November 2025 with government decision expected in July 2026 (now). The LGR risk register identifies 6 high-rated risks spanning financial planning, governance, workforce capacity and programme delivery. The council is concurrently developing a 'legacy plan' to deliver corporate priorities through March 2028 if reorganisation proceeds.
findings.matters: Reorganisation creates material uncertainty over the council's future structure, resources and financial management capacity, directly affecting debt servicing and spending predictability
findings.figures: 6 high-rated LGR risks; LGR proposal submitted November 2025; legacy plan to run until March 2028
findings.quote: The June 2026 review of the LGR risk register identifies 6 risks that are currently rated as 'high' and therefore above the Council's risk tolerance threshold. These risks reflect the uncertainty and complexity associated with the reorganisation process, including the need to maintain effective services and governance arrangements while preparing for potential changes to structures, resources, responsibilities and future delivery models.

findings.paper_title: Annual Governance Statement
findings.headline: LGR costs being funded from a reserve established during the year to manage structural transition.
findings.detail: The Council established a reserve to fund the costs of Local Government Reorganisation and has replenished it. This is intended to provide a source of funding to meet LGR costs as the council prepares for vesting day on 1 April 2028. The reserve is being monitored regularly and legacy plans are embedded in the Council's financial plans.
findings.matters: The need to establish and replenish a reserve specifically for reorganisation costs indicates material financial impact; the adequacy of the reserve is unknown and depends on transition costs that are still emerging.
findings.figures: Reserve established and replenished; amount not disclosed in this document
findings.quote: A reserve has been established to provide a source of funding to meet LGR costs and the legacy plans are costed and embedded in the Council's financial plans.

findings.paper_title: Annual Governance Statement
findings.headline: Secretary of State withdrew the Council's planning determination powers for major developments on 16 June 2026, with unknown reputational and financial consequences.
findings.detail: Post year-end, the Council was designated as 'not adequately performing' under planning law. Developers with major schemes (housing >10 homes, sites >0.5 hectares, buildings >1,000 sqm, or land >1 hectare) now bypass the Council entirely; applications go to the Planning Inspectorate instead. The Council recognised this risk and implemented training and improvements, but the withdrawal occurred anyway.
findings.matters: Loss of planning authority signals regulatory failure to external stakeholders; the Council loses fee income and control over local development; reputational damage could affect borrowing capacity and investor confidence.
findings.figures: Applications for major developments over 10 homes, 0.5 hectares, 1,000 sqm, or 1 hectare now determined by Planning Inspectorate, not Council
findings.quote: Post year-end (16 June 2026), the Secretary of State for Housing, Communities and Local Government withdrew the Council's powers to determine planning applications for major developments over 'inadequate' performance under section 62A of the Town and Country Planning Act 1990 and determined the Council was 'not adequately performing' its function of determining applications for planning permission for major development under the 1990 Act. This will have a reputational and financial consequence for the Council which is unknown at the time of writing.

findings.paper_title: Annual Governance Statement
findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation creating structural uncertainty and costs, with central government funding changes anticipated after one-off 2026/27 grants.
findings.detail: The Council is preparing for potential reorganisation by 31 March 2028, which will end its Alliance with High Peak Borough Council. The government decision on the preferred configuration was expected July 2026. The Council is incurring costs already, with costs expected to increase as vesting day approaches. Central government funding changes are being mitigated by one-off grants in 2026/27 but are uncertain in future years.
findings.matters: Structural reorganisation creates financial uncertainty for the council and its lenders; one-off grants masking funding cuts is unsustainable, and the growing costs of transition are not fully quantified.
findings.figures: One-off grants in 2026/27 only; costs to increase as vesting day (1 April 2028) approaches; reserve established but amount not stated
findings.quote: Separate but related facets of LGR are changes to central government funding, negative impacts of which were mitigated by one-off grants in 2026/27 but are uncertain in future.

findings.paper_title: MTFP report, 04/02/2026 Finance and Performance Committee, 10/02/2026 Cabinet
findings.headline: Council will incur greater costs than anticipated last year due to funding cuts and inflation drag
findings.detail: The Council explicitly states it will face higher costs than originally forecast in the prior year's MTFP, driven by both reduced government funding (Fair Funding 2.0 Review cuts) and cumulative inflation effects. Pay awards are forecast at 3% for 2026/27 and 2.5% for 2027/28, with non-payroll inflation also built in.
findings.matters: Signals that cost pressures are outpacing the efficiency strategy, which remains at the same level despite these increased headwinds
findings.figures: 3% pay award 2026/27, 2.5% for 2027/28, 2% thereafter; no quantified cost gap stated
findings.quote: The Council will incur greater costs than anticipated originally in setting the MTFP last year as a result of the funding cuts and effects of inflation 'drag' on Council budgets

findings.paper_title: MTFP report, 04/02/2026 Finance and Performance Committee, 10/02/2026 Cabinet
findings.headline: Staffordshire Moorlands ceases as a separate entity in 2028/29 under Local Government Reorganisation
findings.detail: The final two years of the MTFP (2028/29 and 2029/30) fall outside the life of the current council. These years are included only as memorandum items to demonstrate financial viability at the point of service transfer to a new Unitary Authority. The new authority will be responsible for budgeting from that point forward.
findings.matters: Structural dissolution creates transition risk, uncertainty over service continuity, and potential gaps in financial accountability during reorganisation
findings.figures: 2028/29 dissolution date; additional £475,000 added to final two memorandum years
findings.quote: Under the Government's timetable for Local Government Reorganisation, the last two years of the MTFP (2028/29 and 2029/30) will fall outside the life of Staffordshire Moorlands District Council

findings.paper_title: MTFP report, 04/02/2026 Finance and Performance Committee, 10/02/2026 Cabinet
findings.headline: Employer's National Insurance grant funding fell significantly short of actual costs incurred in 2025/26
findings.detail: The Council's pay award in 2025/26 matched budget assumptions, but government ENI grant funding was materially lower than the costs the Council actually incurred. This represents a real funding gap that emerged between assumption and reality, not just a planning error.
findings.matters: Shows a systematic gap between government funding assumptions and actual costs, creating unexpected deficits and exposing forecasting risk
findings.figures: Not quantified in the document
findings.quote: the amount of Employer's National Insurance grant funding the Council received fell significantly short of the costs actually incurred

findings.paper_title: Appendix A (Finance) for 2026/27 to 2029/30 Medium Term Financial Plan & 2026/27 Budget Setting
findings.headline: Borrowing costs rising steeply; net cost of capital shifts from £266k surplus to £672k annual cost by 2029/30
findings.detail: PWLB borrowing rates are forecast at 4.60% initially, expected to fall to 4.10%. The Council's capital programme requires £24.4m borrowing over five years. Despite investment income, net borrowing costs shift from a net surplus position of £266k in 2025/26 (where investment income exceeds borrowing costs) to a net annual cost of £672k by 2029/30. This represents a structural shift in the council's interest-rate exposure and cost of capital.
findings.matters: Rising interest costs reduce the council's operating margin and constrain its ability to afford new debt. If interest rates remain higher than forecast or capital needs increase, the council's budget assumptions will deteriorate rapidly, forcing reserve depletion.
findings.figures: Net borrowing cost/(income): 2025/26 (£265,910) surplus to 2029/30 £672,100 cost; PWLB borrowing rates forecast 4.60% decreasing to 4.10%; borrowing costs rising 2025/26 £783,120 to 2029/30 £1,508,930
findings.quote: These relatively high interest rates have a significant impact on borrowing costs, partially offset where portfolio sizes allow, by increased investment income.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A (Finance) for 2026/27 to 2029/30 Medium Term Financial Plan & 2026/27 Budget Setting
findings.headline: General reserve headroom shrinking from £494k to £320k over the plan period; reserves already drawn down 34% in prior year
findings.detail: The council's contingency reserves are forecast to decline from £1.954m in 2026/27 to £1.669m by 2029/30 against a minimum required level of £1.349m. Headroom above minimum falls from £494k to £320k. Reserves were already materially drawn down from £2.690m in March 2024 to £2.226m by March 2025 due to in-year outturn, further compressing the buffer available for unexpected events.
findings.matters: A council's general reserves are its only cushion against unexpected events or shortfalls in income. Declining headroom means less capacity to absorb cost pressures or revenue shocks without drawing reserves below the CFO's recommended minimum, increasing default risk.
findings.figures: Contingency reserve forecast: 2026/27 opening £1,954,410 (headroom £605,410), 2029/30 £1,669,090 (headroom £320,090); prior year drawdown: £2.690m (2024) to £2.226m (2025)
findings.quote: Following the 2024/25 outturn position and a net use of reserves, the Council general fund contingency balance at 31 March 2025 stood at £1.760million (£2.690million at 31 March 2024). The updated MTFP shows a forecast cumulative deficit position of £285,320 over the four years, which represents the anticipated net contribution to contingency reserves in maintaining a balanced 4-year plan.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A (Finance) for 2026/27 to 2029/30 Medium Term Financial Plan & 2026/27 Budget Setting
findings.headline: Strategic Alliance with High Peak Borough Council ending 31 March 2028, removing shared service efficiency benefits
findings.detail: The Council operates a Strategic Alliance with High Peak Borough Council that has delivered efficiency savings through joint management and services. This arrangement must end on 31 March 2028 as a consequence of LGR. The MTFP does not yet quantify what service disruption or cost increase will result from dissolution of the Alliance.
findings.matters: The end of a shared service arrangement removes economies of scale and efficiencies the council has been capturing. The MTFP does not yet identify transition costs or quantify the higher cost base post-dissolution, suggesting material unknown liabilities.
findings.figures: Alliance dissolution date: 31 March 2028
findings.quote: The Council maintains a Strategic Alliance with High Peak Borough Council, formed around the principle of shared services in the pursuit of efficiency and realisation of savings. The Strategic Alliance has enabled the implementation and transformation of a joint management structure and services, consequently realising significant efficiency savings. The implications of LGR mean that this arrangement will come to an end on 31 March 2028 and the Council must plan for the cessation of the Alliance in that timeframe.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A (Finance) for 2026/27 to 2029/30 Medium Term Financial Plan & 2026/27 Budget Setting
findings.headline: Efficiency savings programme significantly underperforming against target; £267k cumulative shortfall
findings.detail: The council is failing to hit its efficiency targets. As of 2025/26, it shows a cumulative shortfall of £267,080 against planned savings. The most concerning area is Council Controlled Companies (contracted service AES), which was expected to deliver £557,000 over the plan period but is falling materially short. The paper describes this as only 'moderate success' and does not yet quantify how shortfalls will be recovered.
findings.matters: If planned savings are not being achieved, the council is relying on reserves to balance the budget. This reduces financial resilience and suggests that future efficiency assumptions may also not land, putting pressure on service quality or forcing deeper cuts later.
findings.figures: Cumulative shortfall against MTFP target 2025/26: £267,080; Efficiency target £250,000 but only £141,480 achieved in year; Council Controlled Companies planned £557,000 total savings but fell short in 2024/25
findings.quote: Achievements to date show moderate success against the plan. The significant savings target assigned to the Council Controlled Companies, which was focussed on AES in the first year, did not reach the target during the year.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A (Finance) for 2026/27 to 2029/30 Medium Term Financial Plan & 2026/27 Budget Setting
findings.headline: Levelling Up Fund capital projects running over budget and behind schedule, consuming reserves
findings.detail: Two major capital schemes funded by the Levelling Up Fund are experiencing cost overruns and delays. Brough Park Leisure Centre has added £1.1m to its budget due to electricity network upgrades and has been delayed past its scheduled opening. Nicholson Institute has added £0.2m. Both increases have been absorbed from the Council's LUF capital reserve, weakening its ability to manage future project risks.
findings.matters: Project overruns consume reserves and suggest project delivery challenges. For a lender, this indicates weakening capital delivery capability during a period of organisational transition, increasing the risk of further slippage.
findings.figures: Brough Park Leisure Centre additional budget £1.1m (including £0.46m for external landscaping and signage); Nicholson Institute additional budget £0.2m; both met from Council's capital LUF reserve
findings.quote: Brough Park Leisure Centre re-development has been substantially completed but works to upgrade the electricity network has delayed the opening. Additional budget of £1.1m has been incorporated for the project in this update this includes £0.46m for external landscaping and signage works which are part funded from Sports England.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A (Finance) for 2026/27 to 2029/30 Medium Term Financial Plan & 2026/27 Budget Setting
findings.headline: Council entering Local Government Reorganisation with uncertain costs, timescale, and successor entity financial viability
findings.detail: The council is merging into a new authority under Local Government Reorganisation, with the merger date and configuration unknown until summer 2026. The MTFP includes provisional financial provisions for external HR support, staff training, and ICT transition, but explicitly states these are estimates and 'further costs will become apparent as the process starts to emerge'. The plan also ends on 2028/29 when the merger occurs, making the final year notional.
findings.matters: LGR introduces execution risk: transition costs may overrun, service continuity may be disrupted, and the merged authority's financial viability is unknown at the time of borrowing decisions. A lender needs to understand whether this borrower will continue to exist and on what terms.
findings.figures: External HR support including Local Government Reorganisation £123,000 (2026/27), net (£100,000) by 2028/29; staff training commitment £16,000 (2026/27)
findings.quote: This MTFP represents the start of the transition process, with the first half of the Plan representing the final years of Staffordshire Moorlands District Council; and the second half representing the first years of the successor authority; details of which will not be fully known until the Summer of 2026. There are some significant risks evolving in connection with the LGR process including the timing, the cost and the resource the Council has to deliver the transition; whilst at the same time maintaining high quality services within the Staffordshire Moorlands.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A (Finance) for 2026/27 to 2029/30 Medium Term Financial Plan & 2026/27 Budget Setting
findings.headline: Gross government funding declining £3.081m over the medium term from Fair Funding Review reset
findings.detail: The Fair Funding Review 2.0 and reset of the Business Rates Retention Scheme represent structural changes to how central government funds local authorities. The paper explicitly quantifies the loss: consolidated grants fall in value terms and Revenue Support Grant drops from £4.3m to £2.2m by year 3 of the plan. The paper notes this is a redistribution away from this authority.
findings.matters: Structural reductions in central funding mean the council cannot rely on future funding growth and must manage within a shrinking resource envelope. This constrains the council's ability to service debt and absorb cost shocks.
findings.figures: Fair Funding 2.0 review decrease in gross funding: (£3.081million); Revenue Support Grant: 2025/26 £123,310 to 2026/27 £4,327,040 then £2,200,000 (2028/29)
findings.quote: The Fair Funding 2.0 review and multi-year provisional Local Government Finance Settlement shows a decrease in gross funding: (£3.081million)

findings.paper_title: Appendix A (Finance) for 2026/27 to 2029/30 Medium Term Financial Plan & 2026/27 Budget Setting
findings.headline: Government funding cut of £3.5m in 2026/27 alone from Business Rates reset
findings.detail: The Business Rates Retention Scheme is being reset from 1 April 2026, with the Council's Baseline Funding Level falling sharply. Year-on-year funding drops from £5.5m to £2.0m, representing a loss of £3.5m in this single line of income. This reflects a structural reduction in the Council's government funding assigned by the Fair Funding Review, not a one-off adjustment.
findings.matters: A permanent loss of this scale in core government funding forces difficult choices on service levels or reserves. Lenders assess whether a council can service debt from recurring income that is shrinking.
findings.figures: Business Rates Retention: 2025/26 £5,502,050 to 2026/27 £1,994,730; change year-on-year £3,507,320 reduction
findings.quote: The Council has been assigned a new Business Rates Baseline (BRB), Baseline Funding Level (BFL) and Tariff amount. To protect the Council's income during the transition to the new arrangements, the Government is increasing the safety net threshold (where the Council's share of Non-Domestic Rating Income (NDRI) is below the BFL) to 100% for 2026/27, reducing to 97% in 2027/28 and 92.5% in 2028/29.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B (Capital Strategy) for 2026/27 to 2029/30 Medium Term Financial Plan & 2026/27 Budget Setting
findings.headline: Council has taken actions to manage affordability, citing uncertainty about the longer-term sustainability of capital plans
findings.detail: The council has formally agreed a range of mitigating actions (asset rationalisation, shared use of assets, reduction in specification, generating capital receipts and additional revenue) specifically to address 'uncertainty of affordability for the longer term plan'.
findings.matters: An explicit statement that affordability is a material concern guides the council's capital strategy and suggests limited headroom for new investment or spending shocks
findings.figures: No specific figures; strategic land review outcomes reflected in revised programme funding but values not stated
findings.quote: In order to address the uncertainty of affordability for the longer term plan, the Council agreed to a number of actions to reduce the impact of the necessary capital spending, which should be considered before investment in each of the assets is made

findings.paper_title: Appendix B (Capital Strategy) for 2026/27 to 2029/30 Medium Term Financial Plan & 2026/27 Budget Setting
findings.headline: Major leisure centre refurbishment programme identified where capital costs significantly exceed any revenue savings
findings.detail: The Future Leisure Provision review identified the need for major investment including replacement of South Moorlands Leisure Centre and refurbishment of Biddulph Valley. The document explicitly states the indicative capital cost is significantly in excess of revenue savings, requiring identification of additional capital funding or cost reductions to proceed.
findings.matters: This indicates an invest-to-save scheme that does not pay for itself from revenue, requiring the council to find additional capital resources or reduce the scope of necessary modernisation
findings.figures: Leisure investment 2026/27: £580k; five-year total £1.2m (but full refurbishment programme costs not itemised)
findings.quote: The indicative capital cost for these investments is significantly in excess of revenue savings. Consequently, it will be necessary for the Council to identify additional sources of capital investment or reductions in the capital costs, to deliver these improvements.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B (Capital Strategy) for 2026/27 to 2029/30 Medium Term Financial Plan & 2026/27 Budget Setting
findings.headline: Strategic Alliance with High Peak ends 31 March 2028, eliminating a major source of efficiency savings
findings.detail: The council has operated a joint management structure and services with High Peak under a Strategic Alliance that has realised significant efficiency savings. This partnership terminates in 2028 due to Local Government Reorganisation, requiring the council to plan for cessation and loss of those savings.
findings.matters: The loss of an efficiency partnership will directly impact the council's cost base and financial sustainability just as it faces continued fiscal pressure
findings.figures: No specific figure given for the value of savings lost
findings.quote: The Strategic Alliance has enabled the implementation and transformation of a joint management structure and services, consequently realising significant efficiency savings. The implications of LGR mean that this arrangement will come to an end on 31 March 2028

findings.paper_title: Staffordshire Moorlands District Council - Audit Findings Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Payroll control assurances from outsourced provider Stoke City Council not received (repeated from prior year)
findings.detail: The Council outsources payroll to Stoke City Council under a service level agreement but has not obtained adequate assurances from Stoke City Council's internal audit on control effectiveness over the MyPayroll system. Although the auditors note high-level controls at Staffordshire Moorlands mitigate the risk, this recommendation was repeated from the prior year.
findings.matters: Lack of assurances from a third-party service provider over a critical financial process indicates either weak contract management or gaps in documented evidence of payroll control effectiveness, a key area lenders assess.
findings.figures: Not specified in report
findings.quote: The Authority were not able to confirm the extent of reporting of operating controls effectiveness over payroll system controls. The Authority has engaged with the Internal Audit Department at Stoke City Council, however such assurances have not been provided.

findings.paper_title: Staffordshire Moorlands District Council - Audit Findings Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Expenditure cycle testing identified £55k extrapolated misstatement in other service expenditure
findings.detail: Auditors tested a sample of other service expenditure and identified three errors: two items that could not be confirmed against supporting evidence (£24.85 and £261.79 differences) and one item of £2.9k that could not be confirmed. This resulted in an extrapolated misstatement of £55k representing potential overstatement of other service expenditure.
findings.matters: Errors in expenditure recording suggest control weaknesses in procurement and payment processes; an extrapolated £55k overstatement indicates systematic issues that could hide cost control problems and service spending drift.
findings.figures: Extrapolated misstatement £55k; individual sample items £24.85, £261.79, £2.9k
findings.quote: We have tested a sample of other service expenditure through to supporting evidence and identified 3 errors. 2 items we were unable to confirm the accuracy of the expenditure recorded on the ledger resulting in differences of (£24.85) and £261.79. One item where we were unable to confirm an amount in the ledger of £2.9k to supporting evidence. In totality this has resulted in an extrapolated misstatement of £55k which is a potential overstatement of other service expenditure.

findings.paper_title: Staffordshire Moorlands District Council - Audit Findings Report 2024-25
findings.headline: £69k write-back of abandoned capital projects incorrectly classified as disposal not impairment
findings.detail: The Council wrote back £69k of assets under construction for abandoned capital projects but incorrectly classified it in the Comprehensive Income and Expenditure Statement as 'derecognition and disposal' rather than as an impairment within cost of services as required by IAS 16 and IAS 36. Net impact on expenditure is nil but misclassification indicates accounting treatment weakness.
findings.matters: Misclassification of capital write-offs obscures the true nature of capital spending failure and impairment, which lenders and directors need to assess capital discipline and whether the council can manage major projects to completion.
findings.figures: £69k of assets under construction written back; net impact on expenditure nil
findings.quote: In addition, the Authority wrote back £69k of assets under construction relating to abandoned capital projects. As a result, this was included in the CIES within 'other operating expenditure' as 'derecognition and disposal value of fixed assets'. Under IAS 16 and IAS36 this amount should have been recognised in the expenditure within 'cost of services' as an impairment.

findings.paper_title: Staffordshire Moorlands District Council - Audit Findings Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Asset register not consistently updated to reflect disposed, demolished or derecognised assets
findings.detail: Auditors identified that the Council does not consistently update its fixed asset register when assets have been disposed of, demolished or derecognised. Assets continued to be included in the register when no longer held by the Authority, creating a risk around asset existence and accuracy of the Council's rights and obligations.
findings.matters: Inaccurate asset registers undermine the reliability of financial reporting and asset management, suggesting control weaknesses that could allow material misstatements in capital expenditure and valuations to pass undetected.
findings.figures: Land and buildings valuation £22.565m at 31 March 2025 (decrease of £5.367m from prior year)
findings.quote: We have raised an improvement recommendation in our 'Action Plan' in section 06 relating to the maintenance of the fixed asset register as our audit work identified that the Authority is not consistency updating its asset register to reflect assets which have been disposed of, demolished or derecognised. We identified instances where assets continued to be included in the register when they had been disposed of or derecognised.

findings.paper_title: Staffordshire Moorlands District Council - Audit Findings Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Segregation of duties weakness: finance staff hold both journal processing and administrator access rights
findings.detail: Auditors identified that several finance team members have the ability to both process journals and hold administrator access rights in financial systems. This creates a risk around segregation of duties and potential for inappropriate user activity without compensating controls.
findings.matters: Weak segregation of duties in financial systems increases the risk of undetected fraud or error in financial reporting, and is a control weakness that lenders assess when evaluating management's oversight.
findings.figures: 39,409 journals posted during the year; 33 journals tested for management override risk
findings.quote: We also identified a number of staff in the finance team who are able to process journals and have administrator access rights which has been detailed further as part of our other findings relating to IT in Section 04 of the report. This creates a risk around the segregation of duties and potential inappropriate user activity.

findings.paper_title: Staffordshire Moorlands District Council - Audit Findings Report 2024-25
findings.headline: £231k understatement of investment property valuation due to buyer's costs deduction
findings.detail: The external valuer incorrectly deducted buyer's costs (stamp duty and similar) from the investment property valuation, resulting in an understatement of £231k. This represents an absolute error across the entire investment property balance. The Council has not adjusted the financial statements, treating it as immaterial.
findings.matters: Investment properties worth £4.623m generate rental income for the council; incorrect valuations understate the asset base and capital available, affecting assessments of borrowing capacity and asset performance.
findings.figures: Investment property understatement £231k; total investment property value £4.623m
findings.quote: Our detailed testing has identified an understatement of the valuation of £231k as a result of buyer's costs being deducted. This is an absolute error as we tested the entire investment property balance. The misstatement has not been adjusted by management on the grounds of materiality.

findings.paper_title: Staffordshire Moorlands District Council - Audit Findings Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Material increase in pension liability of £1.14m requiring financial statements amendment
findings.detail: Auditors requested the Council obtain a revised IAS19 report from the actuary as the original did not include an updated IFRIC 14 impact assessment. The revised report increased the pension liability by £1.14m and reduced the remeasurement in the comprehensive income and expenditure statement from £3.331m to £2.190m. The Council adjusted its financial statements for this finding.
findings.matters: A £1.14m material adjustment to the pension liability (now £11.166m) is significant to the overall financial position and affects the accuracy of usable reserves available to the council.
findings.figures: Pension liability £11.166m at 31 March 2025; increased by £1.14m; remeasurement adjusted from £3.331m to £2.190m
findings.quote: We identified a material adjustment impacting the primary statements and disclosures in relation to this significant risk. We requested the Authority obtain a revised IAS19 report from the actuary as the report reflected in the financial statements although updated for the actual investment returns at 31.3.25 did not include an updated IFRIC 14 impact assessment. This increased the pensions liability by £1.14m and reduced the remeasurement taken to the CIES from £3.331m to £2.190m.

news_drafts.lead: Internal borrowing depletes the council's liquid reserves and creates refinancing risk if rates do not fall, potentially forcing expensive external borrowing later.

news_drafts.lead: Lower-than-expected investment returns reduce the council's capacity to self-fund services and increase dependency on borrowing or reserves.
